title: Vasishtha asks, what did I do?
hookLine: a friend goes quiet. In a Rig Veda hymn, the seer Vasishtha goes to Varuna and asks: what did I do? Why Hindus still ask forgiveness at the end of puja
carry: a wrong breaks rita; honest asking mends it
tomorrow: a nurse walks out at dawn. what did the poets sing to it?

cards: The messages used to come every day. Jokes, photos, long voice notes. Now a friend answers in one word, or not at all.
Something happened, but what? You scroll back looking for the moment it changed. A mutual friend shrugs: seems like they're upset with you.
So there's one honest move left, and it's the hardest: go to the friend and ask, what did I do? A Rig Veda poet makes exactly that move, and the one he asks is a god.

teach.h: VARUNA KEEPS RITA, THE RIGHT ORDER.
teach.b: The god is Varuna. In the hymns, Varuna keeps rita, the right order of things, and he sees what people do. The poet is Vasishtha, a seer tradition remembers as the voice of these hymns.

In paraphrase, Vasishtha says: I ask about this wrong, Varuna, wanting to understand. I go to the wise to ask, and the sages all tell me the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. So he turns to Varuna himself.
What was my great offense, he asks, that you would strike the friend who sings your praise? Tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing, free of it.
He asks to be released from the wrongs of his fathers, and from the ones he did himself. Then this. It wasn't my own will, Varuna.
It was drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness. The older one leads the younger astray. Even sleep doesn't keep wrongdoing away.
Some readers hear an excuse in that. Others hear a man naming his weak spots out loud. Either way, he doesn't hide them.
Here's the teaching under it. For the Vedic poets, a wrong isn't only a broken rule.

teach.h: OWN IT, ASK, BE SET RIGHT.
teach.b: It knocks rita, the right order that holds the world together, out of true, and it strains a bond with God, whom Vasishtha calls his friend.

teach.h: A WRONG BREAKS RITA. ASKING MENDS IT.
teach.b: The way back is to own the wrong out loud and ask to be set right. That thread never left Hinduism. Many families still close a puja by asking God's forgiveness for any mistake, known or unknown.

how: Hymns to Varuna are read in Hindu tradition as prayers for release from wrongdoing, and many families still close a puja with a prayer asking God's forgiveness for any mistakes made, known or unknown.

games.q: what does “what the rig veda is” mean?
o: prayers that ask a god to curse an enemy
a list of punishments for breaking the law
hymns of praise, and a seer's honest plea

games.q: Vasishtha and Varuna — tap the pairs.

s: the Rig Veda contains only praise of the gods
in one hymn, Vasishtha asks Varuna what wrong he did, and asks to be released from it.
Vasishtha names his weak spots out loud
drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness: he says these led him astray.
Vasishtha blames the sages for Varuna's anger
the sages only tell him Varuna is angry. he goes to Varuna himself to ask why.

games.q: you're Vasishtha. the wise all tell you the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. what do you do?
o: stay away from Varuna until it blows over.
go to Varuna and ask what you did.
find a different god to praise.
games.why: he asks Varuna directly: what was my offense? tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing.

practice: Do what many families do at the end of a puja: ask forgiveness for what went wrong, known or unknown. Let one strained bond come to mind and, instead of arguing your side, ask quietly: what part of this is mine?
Name it plainly, as Vasishtha named drink and anger and dice. If you pray, bring it to God and ask to be set right; if not, just hold it honestly.

wordCard.voice: What the Rig Veda is. Not only hymns of praise, but a seer asking Varuna what he did wrong, and naming his own weak spots out loud.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Varuna, the Vedic god who keeps rita, the right order, and sees what people do.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: a wrong breaks rita, and honest asking mends it. Even a seer could ask a god, what did I do? Go gently.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 7.86.3–6 (I ask, wishing to know; the sages say Varuna is angry; what was the chief offense; release us from the wrongs of our fathers and our own; it was not our own will: drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness; the older leads the younger astray; even sleep does not ward off wrong)
